items.stem: How many texts does an HL student analyse in Paper 1?
items.answer: Two – both unseen non-literary passages
items.markingKey: D. HL students write on both passages in 2 hours 15 minutes.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Paper 1 at HL and Paper 1 at SL.
items.answer: SL students choose one of two unseen non-literary passages and write one analysis in 1 h 15 (20 marks); HL students analyse both passages in 2 h 15 (40 marks). Both carry 35%.
items.markingKey: SL students choose one of two unseen non-literary passages and write one analysis in 1 h 15 (20 marks); HL students analyse both passages in 2 h 15 (40 marks). Both carry 35%. items.stem: "In Paper 1 you must answer the guiding question exactly as phrased." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The guiding question is optional support; a well-focused analysis of your own is also acceptable.
items.markingKey: The guiding question is optional support; a well-focused analysis of your own is also acceptable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following letter to the editor of a regional newspaper in northern England.

Sir, – Your columnist last week described our local accent as 'charming but unprofessional'. I have been a nurse for twenty-two years. I have said 'you're alright, love' to frightened patients at three in the morning, and not one has asked for my vowels to be adjusted. Accent is not a skill deficit. It is where we come from, and where many of your readers still live.

Which conventions of its text type does this unseen text use, and why?
items.answer: It is a letter. Conventions: a salutation and sign-off, a named addressee, a clearly stated purpose and a request or demand. In this text, for example: "Accent is not a skill deficit. It is where we come from" (antithesis) and the formal opening "Sir, –", each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience.
items.markingKey: It is a letter. Conventions: a salutation and sign-off, a named addressee, a clearly stated purpose and a request or demand. In this text, for example: "Accent is not a skill deficit. It is where we come from" (antithesis) and the formal opening "Sir, –", each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a travel brochure for a tour of Iceland.

Where fire meets ice. Stand where continents drift apart at Thingvellir. Soak beneath the northern lights in steaming geothermal pools. Let the silence of a black-sand beach rewrite your idea of quiet. This isn't a holiday. It's a reset. Small groups. Expert local guides. Carbon-offset flights.

Identify the text type, audience and purpose of this unseen text, giving evidence for each.
items.answer: Affluent travellers seeking adventure and wellbeing, possibly environmentally conscious. To persuade readers to book the tour by presenting Iceland as dramatic, restorative and responsible.
items.markingKey: Affluent travellers seeking adventure and wellbeing, possibly environmentally conscious. To persuade readers to book the tour by presenting Iceland as dramatic, restorative and responsible. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: A student claims: "Paper 1 texts can be literary extracts such as poems." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Paper 1 in Language and Literature uses non-literary texts only; literary works are assessed in Paper 2, the IO and the HL essay.
items.markingKey: Paper 1 in Language and Literature uses non-literary texts only; literary works are assessed in Paper 2, the IO and the HL essay. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how you would spend the first 15 minutes of Paper 1 with an unseen text, and justify each step.
items.answer: Indicative content: read for gist; identify type, audience, purpose, context; annotate features linked to guiding question; formulate thesis; plan paragraphs; justification.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: read for gist; identify type, audience, purpose, context; annotate features linked to guiding question; formulate thesis; plan paragraphs; justification.

items.stem: "The guiding question helps weaker students more than strong ones." Discuss.
items.answer: It helps all students; stronger ones use it as a springboard rather than a limit.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it gives a clear focus; it points to a central feature. Arguments against: strong students also benefit from a focused line of argument; over-reliance can narrow analysis. Supported judgement: It helps all students; stronger ones use it as a springboard rather than a limit. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.answer: It is a support, not a requirement; a student may develop their own focus as long as the analysis addresses how the text creates meaning.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a family SUV, printed in a weekend newspaper magazine.

[Image: a father at the wheel, two children asleep in the back, mountains at dusk through the windscreen.]
HE'S GOT THIS.
Seven seats. Five-star safety. Zero doubts.
The Atlas X7. Built for the man who carries everyone.
[Small print: 7.9 L/100 km combined. Model shown with optional extras.]

What can you infer about the intended audience and purpose of this text?
items.answer: Fathers and middle-income parents reading a weekend magazine, particularly men who see themselves as family providers. To persuade readers to buy the SUV by linking it to safety and to an ideal of dependable fatherhood.

items.stem: A thesis that merely lists three devices is weak because:
options: It does not make an argument about meaning or effect
It is written in the third person
items.answer: It does not make an argument about meaning or effect
items.markingKey: B. A thesis should argue, not list.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a thesis and a topic.
items.answer: A topic is what the text is about (plastic waste); a thesis is an arguable claim about how the text presents that topic and to what effect.
items.markingKey: A topic is what the text is about (plastic waste); a thesis is an arguable claim about how the text presents that topic and to what effect. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "The best way to organise a Paper 1 analysis is to go through the text line by line." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Line-by-line commentary often becomes descriptive; organising by argument (aspects or effects) better shows focus and analysis, though a well-handled sequential approach can work.
items.markingKey: Line-by-line commentary often becomes descriptive; organising by argument (aspects or effects) better shows focus and analysis, though a well-handled sequential approach can work. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph on the visual features of an advertisement, linked to the thesis "The advert sells belonging rather than a product."

items.stem:
Read the following sponsored advertisement for a skincare serum, shown in a social media feed.

Glow like you mean it.
Clinically shown*: 87% saw brighter skin in 14 days.
Powered by Vitamin C-12, our exclusive molecule from Swiss labs.
Because you deserve skin that tells the truth about you.
#NoFilterNeeded – Tap to shop. Free delivery today only.
*Survey of 64 women, self-reported results.

Guiding question: How does the advertisement combine scientific authority and emotional appeal to persuade its audience?
Plan a line of argument for a Paper 1 analysis of this text.
items.answer: Thesis: the advert uses the language of science to make an emotional promise feel factual. (1) The statistic and jargon ("Vitamin C-12", "Swiss labs") create authority. (2) "You deserve" and "tells the truth about you" tie the product to self-worth. (3) The scarcity close and platform conventions convert desire into a tap. Evaluation: the footnote undermines the claim (64 women, self-reported), so the persuasion depends on readers not reading carefully.
items.markingKey: Thesis: the advert uses the language of science to make an emotional promise feel factual. (1) The statistic and jargon ("Vitamin C-12", "Swiss labs") create authority. Evaluation: the footnote undermines the claim (64 women, self-reported), so the persuasion depends on readers not reading carefully. Markbands (criteria A–D). items.stem:
Read the following home-front poster from a fictional wartime nation, written in the style of 1940s propaganda.

[Image: a woman in overalls rolls up her sleeve beside a factory gate; behind her, the silhouettes of marching soldiers.]
THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT.
YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE.
Every shell you make is a letter home.
Don't let them down – report for factory work today.

Guiding question: How does the poster persuade women to take up factory work?
Plan a line of argument for a Paper 1 analysis of this text.
items.answer: Thesis: the poster recruits by equating industrial labour with the soldier's heroism and with love. (1) Parallel capitals equate front and lathe. (2) The metaphor "a letter home" transforms shells into affection. (3) The image of the rolled sleeve models readiness, and the imperative uses guilt. Evaluation: the empowerment is conditional – it serves the war effort rather than women's equality.

items.stem:
Read the following homepage of a fictional university in Singapore, described in words.

[Banner photograph: four smiling students of different ethnicities walk across a sunlit lawn; one carries a robotic arm.]
Headline: 'Shape What's Next.'
Menu bar: Study | Research | Life on Campus | Apply Now – 'Apply Now' is an orange button, the only coloured item.
Scrolling ticker: 'Ranked #1 in Asia for graduate employability*'.
Pop-up chat window: 'Hi! I'm Ava, your student guide. What would you like to discover today?'

Note in your plan how the single orange "Apply Now" button contributes to the text's purpose.
items.answer: The single orange "Apply Now" button: colour contrast directs the eye to the desired action.
items.markingKey: The single orange "Apply Now" button: colour contrast directs the eye to the desired action. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). items.stem: Kwame writes: "Planning wastes time in a timed exam." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A short plan improves focus and organisation (criterion C) and usually saves time during writing.

items.stem: Annotate a short non-literary text of your choice (described in words) and produce a plan for a Paper 1 response.

Organising points and evidence into a structured outline before writing
The Paper 1 task: an analysis of an unseen non-literary text, supported by a guiding question

items.markingKey: C. "planning" is organising points and evidence into a structured outline before writing.

items.stem: You have 2 hours 15 minutes for HL Paper 1. Propose a time plan for both texts.
items.answer: For example: about 67 minutes per text – roughly 15 minutes reading and planning, 47 minutes writing, 5 minutes checking each; justification.
items.markingKey: For example: about 67 minutes per text – roughly 15 minutes reading and planning, 47 minutes writing, 5 minutes checking each; justification.

items.stem:
Read the following text.

My grandmother's street in Alfama now has eleven bakeries and no neighbours. The bakeries sell pastéis de nata to people who will leave on Sunday; the neighbours who once bought bread there have left for good, priced out by short-term rentals. Tourism, we are told, is our salvation. Perhaps. But a city that sells its every doorway eventually has nothing left to show its visitors except itself, emptied.

Identify the text type of the extract above.
items.answer: opinion column
items.markingKey: B. It is a opinion column: it uses conventions such as a by-lined, first-person argument on a topical issue, a hook, evidence and anecdote, concession and a clear stance.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a campaigner for women's suffrage at a public meeting in Manchester, 1912 (an original pastiche written for study).

Gentlemen of the press, you call us unreasonable. Very well. Was it reasonable that my mother paid taxes on a shop she ran for thirty years, yet could not vote for the men who spent them? Was it reasonable that the law counted her as a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing? We have asked politely for forty years. Politeness has been answered with silence. We shall not be silent any longer.

As part of your timed annotation, explain how "a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing" could support an answer to the guiding question: "How does the speaker turn the accusation of being "unreasonable" against her opponents?"
items.answer: Antithesis: "a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing" – the balanced contrast exposes the contradiction in how the law treated women.
items.markingKey: Antithesis: "a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing" – the balanced contrast exposes the contradiction in how the law treated women. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

Read the following three-panel comic strip, described in words.

[Panel 1: a world leader at a podium declares, 'We pledge to reach net zero by 2050!' Applause lines fill the background.]

items.stem:
Read the following pair of headlines and opening lines from two newspapers reporting the same student protest.

Newspaper A: 'Thousands of students march for affordable housing' – Students filled the city centre on Saturday, chanting and carrying handmade banners, to demand rent controls.
Newspaper B: 'Student mob brings city centre to standstill' – Shoppers were left stranded on Saturday as crowds of students blocked roads, causing chaos for local businesses.

Before writing a Paper 1 analysis, record the audience and purpose of this text with supporting evidence.
items.answer: Readers of two newspapers with different political leanings. Both inform readers of the protest, but each frames it to shape the reader's attitude – sympathetic (A) or hostile (B).

items.stem: A student claims: "Planning wastes time in a timed exam." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A short plan improves focus and organisation (criterion C) and usually saves time during writing.

items.stem:
Read the following donation page on an animal-rescue charity's website, described in words.

[Photograph: a one-eyed dog looks straight into the camera.]
'Meet Biscuit. He was found tied to a motorway barrier in January.'
Progress bar: 'This month: 8,450 euros of 10,000 raised.'
Buttons: 10 | 25 | 50 | Other. A pre-ticked box: 'Make this a monthly gift'.
Footer: '94 cents of every euro goes directly to animal care.'

Guiding question: How does the web page use its design and language to encourage donations?
Write a thesis and a topic sentence for each of your body paragraphs.
items.answer: Thesis: the page combines an emotional story with interface "nudges". (1) The named dog and direct gaze. (2) Emotive detail. (3) Progress bar, button order and pre-ticked box. Evaluation: the default monthly gift may manipulate donors.
items.markingKey: Thesis: the page combines an emotional story with interface "nudges". (1) The named dog and direct gaze. (2) Emotive detail. (3) Progress bar, button order and pre-ticked box. Evaluation: the default monthly gift may manipulate donors. Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem:
Read the following single-panel editorial cartoon, described in words.

[A giant smartphone towers over a family dinner table like a skyscraper. The parents and two children sit at its base, each gazing up at its glowing screen. Their plates are untouched. Under the table, the family dog looks up at the reader. Speech bubble from the dog: 'Remember when they used to drop food?']

Write two annotations on the quotation "A giant smartphone towers over a family dinner table like a skyscraper" that you could develop in a Paper 1 response.
items.answer: Exaggeration (hyperbole): "A giant smartphone towers over a family dinner table like a skyscraper" – the absurd scale shows the phone's dominance over family life.
items.markingKey: Exaggeration (hyperbole): "A giant smartphone towers over a family dinner table like a skyscraper" – the absurd scale shows the phone's dominance over family life. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following three-panel comic strip, described in words.

[Panel 1: a world leader at a podium declares, 'We pledge to reach net zero by 2050!' Applause lines fill the background.]
[Panel 2: a polar bear on a shrinking ice floe raises a paw: 'Question – what's the plan for this summer?']
[Panel 3: the leader, sweating, looks away: 'Next question.']

Which conventions of its text type does this unseen text use, and why?
items.answer: It is a cartoon. Conventions: a single image or panels, caricature, captions or speech bubbles and visual exaggeration for comment. In this text, for example: "a polar bear on a shrinking ice floe raises a paw" (anthropomorphism) and the three-panel set-up, question and punchline, each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience.

items.stem:
Read the following food blog post by a second-generation Ghanaian-British writer.

My mum never measured anything. 'Small pepper,' she'd say, and my eyes would water for an hour. Writing her jollof recipe down for you feels like a betrayal – like pinning a butterfly. But she is getting older, and I am scared of forgetting. So here it is, in grams and millilitres, with all the love that won't fit in brackets.

Note in your plan how the move from memory to present fear ("But she is getting older") contributes to the text's purpose.
items.answer: The move from memory to present fear ("But she is getting older"): the turn explains why the writer overcomes her reluctance.
items.markingKey: The move from memory to present fear ("But she is getting older"): the turn explains why the writer overcomes her reluctance. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The guiding question helps weaker students more than strong ones."
items.answer: It helps all students; stronger ones use it as a springboard rather than a limit.

Arguments against: strong students also benefit from a focused line of argument; over-reliance can narrow analysis. Supported judgement: It helps all students; stronger ones use it as a springboard rather than a limit.

items.stem: "A strong thesis is more important than detailed analysis in Paper 1." Discuss.
items.answer: Both are essential: the thesis organises and detailed analysis proves.
